title: Forced Oscillations
experiment: Sweeping the driving frequency ω shows the steady-state amplitude A of Eq. 15.29 peaking at the natural frequency ω_0. Raising the damping b lowers and widens that peak, which is the document's resonance claim (Figure 15.31).
archetype_reason: the claim is about the shape of the closed-form amplitude A(ω) in Eq. 15.29 and how damping changes it, so no time stepping is needed

fixed.curve_grid: A(ω) evaluated at 3000 evenly spaced ω from 0 to 3·ω_0 inclusive, for the current b, m, k
fixed.width_rule: the ω where A(ω) first rises above A_max/2 and the ω where it last falls below A_max/2 on the curve grid, found by linear interpolation between grid points

source.quote: Recall that the angular frequency, and therefore the frequency, of the motor can be adjusted.
The highest peak, or greatest response, is for the least amount of damping, because less energy is removed by the damping force.
Attach a mass m to a spring in a viscous fluid
where ω_0=√((k)/(m)) is the natural frequency of the mass/spring system

metrics.name: amplitude
metrics.label: amplitude a
metrics.meaning: steady-state amplitude A from Eq. 15.29 at the current ω, b, m, k with F_0 = 1

metrics.name: width
metrics.label: half-amplitude width Δω
metrics.meaning: on the fixed curve grid, A_max is the largest A(ω); width is the upper half-amplitude crossing minus the lower one, located by the fixed width rule; it does not depend on the current ω

reproduce.claim: Driving at the natural frequency with light damping gives the maximum amplitude F_0/(bω_0) = 10 for m = k = 1, b = 0.1.

source.quote: The maximum amplitude results when the frequency of the driving force equals the natural frequency of the system

contrast.claim: Tripling the damping at the same resonant drive gives a much lower peak and a much wider resonance curve.

source.quote: the widths of the resonance curves shown in Figure 15.31 depend on damping: the less the damping, the narrower the resonance
